title: Trump Keeps Making Threats but the World Has Stopped Flinching
excerpt: After months of dramatic ultimatums that rarely materialize, allies and adversaries alike are treating Trump's escalating rhetoric as background noise rather than genuine threats.
body:
• Trump has threatened Iran at least six times since the April ceasefire without altering Tehran's stance, and markets now largely treat his deadlines as negotiating tactics.
  • Allies in Europe, the Gulf, and Asia have shifted from alarm to strategic hedging, building independent defence capacity rather than relying on Washington's word.
  • The pattern of dramatic escalation followed by sudden reversal — from the 'whole civilization will die' ultimatum to weekend ceasefire announcements — has eroded the deterrent value of American rhetoric.
  • For the Indian diaspora, the credibility gap complicates everything from energy prices and shipping routes to the geopolitical calculus of the US-India relationship.

On August 2, Donald Trump warned of "the biggest attack since World War II" against Iran. By the following day, he was talking about giving Tehran "one last chance" and claiming renewed negotiations were underway. Iran's Foreign Ministry promptly denied any talks were happening.

It was, by now, a familiar pattern. In the five months since the US launched its "Epic Fury" offensive against Iran in late February, the president has claimed victory more than ten times, threatened civilizational destruction, and announced at least six deadlines — none of which produced the capitulation he promised.

The Boy Who Cried Wolf

The turning point came on April 7, when Trump posted on Truth Social that "a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again" unless Iran agreed to a deal by 8 p.m. The ultimatum ricocheted from the Oval Office to foreign embassies and trading floors worldwide. Pope Leo condemned the threat. Democratic lawmakers called the president "completely unhinged." Even Marjorie Taylor Greene, a once-staunch ally, expressed concern.

Less than ninety minutes before the deadline, Trump backed down, announcing a two-week ceasefire.

"Trump's made so many threats without following through, I think the market views his threats as mostly bluster."

— Grégory Brew, Iran specialist, Eurasia Group

Wall Street's reaction was telling. Traders treated the day like other Trump deadlines before it: as a negotiating gambit they largely expected to pass without catastrophe. European officials huddled on a call and "largely convinced themselves that Trump would back off," according to The Wall Street Journal's reporting.

A Stalemate Disguised as Strategy

Since the ceasefire, the president has promised at least six times to hit Iran "very hard" without altering Tehran's fundamental posture. On July 11, he warned of "1,000 missiles locked and loaded." On July 22, he threatened to destroy "one bridge or power plant" every time Iran attacked shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's foreign minister responded simply: "Eye for an eye."

On July 29, Trump told Fox News, "We're going to beat the fucking shit out of them." The US struck command centres and drone sites the next morning. Within days, Iran retaliated with missile attacks on a US base in Jordan and tankers linked to the UAE.

"Trump's feeling his way forward, threatening and talking at the same time, hoping to calm energy markets," Peter Rough of the Hudson Institute told Le Monde. "But the Iranians keep jamming that up."

Global Recalibration

The credibility gap extends far beyond Iran. The Munich Security Report 2026 described Trump as the most powerful figure challenging existing rules and institutions, labelling him a "demolition man" of the post-1945 international order. European leaders have largely stopped waiting for Washington's lead. Denmark responded to Trump's Greenland threats by deploying troops. The EU convened emergency summits and began accelerating independent defence spending.

In the Gulf, allies who once relied on American security guarantees are hedging. Jordan intercepted Iranian missiles entering its airspace independently. The UAE reserved its "full right to respond" after Iranian attacks on tankers — without referencing US coordination.

"Everyone expected Trump to return to office with bluster," Brett Bruen, a former Obama administration foreign policy adviser, told Reuters. "But this bulldozing of the pillars that have long undergirded international stability and security is taking place at an alarming and disruptive pace."

What This Means for India

For India and its diaspora, the pattern carries direct consequences. Energy prices remain volatile as the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes — stays contested. Indian crude oil imports from the Gulf face persistent risk premiums. The broader uncertainty complicates New Delhi's delicate balancing act between deepening ties with Washington and maintaining its own strategic autonomy.

Emily Harding, a former National Security Council Iran director, warned that the on-again, off-again pattern could continue through the US midterm elections in November. "Come mid-November, Trump has very little incentive to hold back," she told USA Today. "There's no incentive for the Iranians to cave at the moment."

What's Next

With Iran denying any active negotiations and Trump alternating between apocalyptic threats and sudden ceasefire announcements, the war appears stuck in a loop. Each cycle further erodes the deterrent value of American rhetoric — leaving the world not so much alarmed as resigned.

As one CNN analysis put it, the presidency is "juggling some of the gravest issues confronted by a modern president" alongside disputes about Washington's Reflecting Pool. Polls show low approval ratings and voter dissatisfaction on the issues that matter most. The world, it seems, has learned to keep scrolling.
nri_angle: The credibility gap in US foreign policy directly affects Indian energy security, Gulf shipping routes, and the strategic calculus of the India-US relationship.
